pedagogy.summary: Interpreting multiplication as SCALING (resizing) rather than only repeated addition: the size of a product relative to a factor depends on whether the OTHER factor is greater than, equal to, or less than 1. Multiplying by 5/3 enlarges, by 1 leaves unchanged, by 2/5 shrinks. This directly confronts the deep-rooted 'multiplication always makes bigger' belief and lets children judge a product's size WITHOUT computing (3/4 × 7 is less than 7 because we take three-quarters of it). It also unifies with equivalence: multiplying by n/n = 1 rescales the name without changing the value.
bestPractices: Teach prediction before calculation: ask whether a product will be bigger or smaller than a factor and WHY, using the size of the multiplier relative to 1.
Directly name and refute 'multiplication makes bigger' — show a <1 multiplier shrinks (3/4 of 7 < 7) and a >1 multiplier grows (5/3 of 7 > 7).
Use a stretch/shrink model (number line, elastic, photo enlargement) so 'scale by' is felt as resizing.
Connect × n/n = ×1 to fraction equivalence: rescaling by a name for 1 keeps the value.
Anchor with benchmarks 0, 1, and the multiplier: compare the multiplier to 1 to decide the direction of change.
keyRepresentations: Number line / elastic band stretched (×>1) or compressed (×<1) relative to the original length
Photo or shape enlargement/reduction by a scale factor
Double number line pairing a quantity with its scaled image
× n/n = ×1 shown as re-partitioning without changing length (equivalence link)
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes the number bigger' (and division always smaller) — predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7 (Fischbein's primitive intuitive model; named explicitly in the IES guide).
Over-corrects to 'any fraction makes it smaller' — predicts 5/3 × 7 < 7 because the multiplier is written as a fraction, ignoring that 5/3 > 1.
Thinks multiplying by n/n changes the value (because 'you multiplied'), not recognising n/n = 1.

learn.summary: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): for a positive quantity, the size of the product relative to that quantity depends on whether the OTHER factor (a positive multiplier) is greater than, equal to, or less than 1. Multiplying 7 by 5/3 enlarges it, by 1 (e.g. 4/4) leaves it unchanged, by 2/5 or 3/4 shrinks it. This confronts the 'multiplication always makes bigger' belief and lets learners judge a product's size WITHOUT computing (3/4 × 7 is part of 7, so less than 7). It also unifies with equivalence: multiplying by n/n = 1 (n not zero) rescales the name without changing the value. Emphasise predicting direction before calculating and comparing the multiplier to 1 — not whether it is written as a fraction.

activities.title: Stretch-and-shrink bar: predict before you scale
feedback: If a learner predicted 'longer' for 3/4 and the bar shrank, reframe as 'three-quarters OF 7' — a part of 7 is less than 7.
When the bar holds at 4/4, point out 4/4 is one whole, so ×4/4 is ×1: the value is unchanged, only re-partitioned.
If a learner expected 5/3 to shrink because 'it's a fraction', have them compare 5/3 to 1: it is more than one whole, so it stretches past 7.
Ask the learner to point to where on the dial the bar switches between shrinking and growing, and name that number (1).
activities.rationale: Scaling is resizing; a model that varies the multiplier across 1 makes the >1/<1 threshold visible and supports predict-first reasoning rather than computation. An interactive dial is one proposed way to make the pivot concrete; a stretched or compressed number line, an elastic band, a double number line pairing a quantity with its scaled image, or a 7 cm photo enlarged/reduced can serve the same purpose. The re-partitioning at 4/4 links scaling to equivalence. These are research-informed proposals, not validated against outcomes.
sourceClaims: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to one factor by the size of the other, and explain that multiplying by a fraction >1 enlarges, =1 leaves unchanged, <1 reduces; relate multiplying a/b by n/n to equivalence.

The misconception that multiplying two numbers must result in a larger number is a common, named misconception that interferes with learning; estimation and reasoning about magnitude (e.g. 1/2 × 1/2 asks for half of a half, so the product is smaller than either factor) are the remedy.
learnerActions: Look at a 7-unit bar placed beside a faint marker of the original length 7.
Before anything moves, predict out loud or in writing whether scaling by a chosen multiplier will make the bar longer, shorter, or the same, and say WHY.
Set the multiplier to 3/4 and watch the bar contract to sit short of 7 (3/4 × 7 = 5.25).
Set the multiplier to 5/3 and watch the bar stretch past 7 (5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67).
Set the multiplier to 4/4 and watch the bar hold exactly at 7, re-partitioned to show it is still the same length.
Sweep the multiplier dial slowly across 1 and notice the exact point where the bar flips from shrinking to growing.
State the rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is more than 1.
activities.intendedInsight: For a positive quantity scaled by a positive multiplier, the product is larger than, equal to, or smaller than the quantity exactly according to whether the multiplier is greater than, equal to, or less than 1 — the number 1 is the pivot, not whether the multiplier is written as a fraction.

activities.title: Predict and sort multipliers by direction
feedback: If a learner picks 'greater, because multiplying always makes bigger', ask when multiplying actually makes a number bigger, steering to the multiplier>1 condition.
If 5/3 is sorted into 'makes smaller', ask them to compare 5/3 with one whole before deciding.
Reward reasons that cite the multiplier's size relative to 1, not reasons that cite 'it's a fraction' or a remembered answer.
activities.rationale: Prediction-and-sort items can surface both the 'always bigger' and the 'any fraction shrinks' errors and give scorable practice on the size-relative-to-1 principle. A sort can check and exercise the direction classification, but on its own it asks for selection rather than independent construction of a reason; pair it with the prediction-and-explanation work.
sourceClaims: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to one factor by the size of the other, and explain that multiplying by a fraction >1 enlarges, =1 leaves unchanged, <1 reduces; relate multiplying a/b by n/n to equivalence.
learnerActions: For each of 3/4 × 7, 5/3 × 7, 2/5 × 7, and 4/4 × 7, predict without calculating whether the product is greater than, less than, or equal to 7, and give a reason.
Sort a set of multipliers into three groups: 'makes bigger', 'leaves the same', 'makes smaller'.
For a prompt such as 'is 3/4 × 7 greater, less than, or equal to 7?', choose and justify an answer, and explain why 'greater, because multiplying makes bigger' is not correct.
Estimate the rough size of a product on a scale before revealing the exact value.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding a product's direction is a comparison of the multiplier to 1, which can be done reliably before any arithmetic.

activities.title: Find the counterexample to 'multiplying always makes bigger'
feedback: Accept a counterexample only if the learner explains why that multiplier shrinks (it is less than 1 / a part of the quantity).
If the corrected rule says 'fractions make it smaller', challenge with 5/3 × 7 and ask them to refine the rule to 'less than 1'.
activities.rationale: Scaling is argument-rich, and critiquing a stated claim lets the learner surface and challenge the misconception by constructing a counterexample and a precise rule. A spoken or written exchange with a character who makes the wrong claim is one proposed way to prompt this; it complements, rather than replaces, seeing the resize on a model.
sourceClaims: 'Multiplication makes bigger, division makes smaller' is a primitive intuitive model children over-generalise from whole-number experience and must be overcome for rational-number operations.

The misconception that multiplying two numbers must result in a larger number is a common, named misconception that interferes with learning; estimation and reasoning about magnitude (e.g. 1/2 × 1/2 asks for half of a half, so the product is smaller than either factor) are the remedy.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'multiplying a number always makes it bigger.'
Find a specific case that shows the claim is false and explain why it fails (e.g. 3/4 × 7 is three-quarters OF 7, so less than 7).
Then state the corrected, precise rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is greater than 1; by 1 it stays the same; by less than 1 it gets smaller.
Explain why 5/3 × 7 does make 7 bigger, so the rule is about size relative to 1, not about being a fraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Refuting the over-generalised belief requires producing a counterexample and restating the condition precisely, which strengthens understanding of why the threshold is 1.

activities.title: Multiplying by n/n keeps the value
feedback: If a learner says 7 × 4/4 is bigger or smaller 'because you multiplied', point out that 4/4 = 1 and that ×1 leaves the quantity unchanged.
Have the learner show the bar holding its length while the partition changes, linking equal length to equal value.
activities.rationale: Treating n/n as 1 ties the scaling view directly to equivalence and addresses the specific belief that any multiplication must change the value. Showing length held constant while re-partitioning makes 'same value, different name' concrete.
sourceClaims: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to one factor by the size of the other, and explain that multiplying by a fraction >1 enlarges, =1 leaves unchanged, <1 reduces; relate multiplying a/b by n/n to equivalence.
learnerActions: Predict what 7 × 4/4 equals and whether it is bigger, smaller, or the same as 7.
Show on a bar or number line that 4/4 is one whole, so the length holds while being re-partitioned into quarters.
Connect this to fraction equivalence: multiplying a/b by n/n (n a whole number greater than 1) gives a different name for the same value.
Explain why 3/4 × 2/2 names the same value as 3/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1: it rescales the name (re-partitions) without changing the value, which is exactly what underlies equivalent fractions.

constraints: Target age roughly 10–11 (Year 5 / Grade 5); conceptual objective, not a computation drill.

Insist on prediction and reasoning BEFORE any calculation — the reason is the diagnostic part. A learner can guess 'less than 7' without understanding; require 'because 3/4 is less than 1, so it's part of 7'.
Always pair a multiplier >1 (e.g. 5/3) with one <1 (e.g. 2/5 or 3/4) so learners must track size relative to 1 rather than applying a blanket 'fractions shrink' rule.
Sorting and multiple-choice items assess direction and can bait errors, but they ask for selection; include tasks where the learner constructs a reason, a counterexample, or a corrected rule.
A static before/after image can show one enlargement and one reduction but does not let the learner vary the multiplier across 1; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main concept-building task.
Keep concrete numbers correct: 3/4 × 7 = 5.25 (short of 7), 5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67 (past 7), 2/5 × 7 = 2.8 (short of 7), 4/4 × 7 = 7.

A zero-thickness on-screen bar or elastic is an idealised model of magnitude/length; physical strips, elastic bands, or photos are approximations with their own properties (slight thickness, stretch limits) — use either to make resizing felt, without claiming one is required or superior.
Compare fractions here as numbers/multipliers against 1; do not teach any 'denominator rule flips' idea — the direction of change comes from the multiplier's size relative to 1.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the IES/WWC practice guide is marked verified in the source row; the CCSS-M 5.NF.5 statement and the Fischbein/Greer claim are marked unverified. Treat the scaling framing and the 'primitive intuitive model' description as resting on unverified citations.

The original labelled a 3D treatment 'poor' because resizing is one-dimensional. That is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; the ranking is dropped, with the neutral observation that extra depth is simply not needed for a length/magnitude resize here.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 × 7 = 5.25, 5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.666…, 2/5 × 7 = 2.8, 4/4 × 7 = 7 — all consistent with the direction claims used in the activities.
The source distractor 'any fraction makes it smaller' is deliberately retained as an error to challenge (via 5/3 > 1), never offered as a correct rule.
The 'bigger only when the multiplier is more than 1' rule is stated for positive quantities, matching the Grade 5 scope of this objective.

assess.poeTask: Before any calculation, show a 7-unit strip (or a photo 7 cm wide). Ask the child to PREDICT what happens to its length when we scale it by 3/4 — longer, shorter, or the same — and to say WHY before anything moves. Then scale it (fold/measure, or reveal 3/4 × 7 = 5.25) and compare. A child holding 'multiplication makes bigger' predicts longer; the strip visibly shrinks to three-quarters of its length. The reason stated before scaling is the diagnostic part — a correct child says 'shorter, because we're taking three-quarters OF it'.
probeDeeper: What does '3/4 of 7' mean — is a part of 7 more or less than 7?
Why is 5/3 × 7 different from 3/4 × 7? What's special about 5/3?
What does multiplying by 4/4 do to a number, and why?
When IS it true that multiplying makes a number bigger? Give me the rule.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/4 × 7 is LESS than 7 (three-quarters OF 7 is part of it, and 3/4 < 1). 5/3 × 7 is BIGGER than 7 (5/3 > 1); 2/5 × 7 is SMALLER than 7 (2/5 < 1). The product's size depends on whether the multiplier is greater or less than 1.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Multiplying always makes the number bigger, so 3/4 × 7 is more than 7' — the primitive multiplication-as-enlargement intuition.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as 'three-quarters OF 7' and show on a stretch model that a <1 multiplier shrinks; ask when multiplying DOES make bigger to surface the multiplier>1 condition.
errorPatterns.distractor: Greater than 7, because multiplying always makes a number bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7, and predicts every multiplier grows the number; reason cites 'times makes bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-corrects: 'multiplying by a fraction makes it smaller, so 5/3 × 7 is less than 7' — treats any fraction multiplier as shrinking, ignoring that 5/3 > 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare 5/3 to 1 (it's more than one whole): scaling by more than one grows the quantity; show 5/3 of 7 stretching past 7 on the model. Distinguish 'a fraction' from 'less than 1'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Smaller, because multiplying by a fraction always makes it smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks multiplying by n/n changes the value because 'you multiplied', not seeing n/n = 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link to equivalence: 4/4 is one whole, so ×4/4 is ×1 — the value is unchanged, only re-partitioned; show the length holding on the model.
errorPatterns.distractor: It changes the value, because you multiplied by something
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 7 × 4/4 (or 3/4 × 2/2) is bigger/smaller than the original rather than equal.

responseLevels.gap: Applies 'multiplication always makes bigger' (predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7) or over-corrects to 'any fraction shrinks it'; no reference to the multiplier's size relative to 1.
responseLevels.full: Predicts without computing that 3/4 × 7 < 7, 5/3 × 7 > 7, 2/5 × 7 < 7, explaining the product's size depends on whether the multiplier is greater or less than 1, and connects × n/n = ×1 to equivalence; transfers to a new multiplier.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts the <1 case correctly but reasons from a memorised 'fractions make it smaller' rule or from having computed, and can't reliably handle the >1 multiplier (5/3) or explain ×n/n = ×1 — lists effects without the unifying 'compare the multiplier to 1' principle.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Without working it out: is 3/4 × 7 greater than 7, less than 7, or equal to 7 — and WHY? Then tell me, again without calculating: does multiplying 7 by 5/3 make it bigger or smaller, and does multiplying 7 by 2/5 make it bigger or smaller?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier is the whole game: a child can guess 'less than 7' but only correct scaling reasoning gives 'because 3/4 is less than 1, so it's part of 7'. Pairing a >1 multiplier (5/3) with a <1 multiplier (2/5) forces the child to track the multiplier's size relative to 1 — something neither 'multiplication makes bigger' (predicts all three grow) nor 'any fraction shrinks it' (predicts 5/3 shrinks) can do. Requiring prediction WITHOUT computing stops a child back-reasoning from an arithmetic answer.
